items.q: A Python script that cleans a 1 GB CSV in 3 minutes now has to handle 100 GB every night. What breaks first, and what do you change?
points: Memory: reading the whole file at once fails; stream it in chunks or with generators
A single core becomes the limit; move the heavy work to DuckDB, Polars or Spark instead of adding threads
The runtime passes the nightly window; partition the input so parts run in parallel and can be retried alone
Name the point where you would stop scaling the script and move to an engine

items.q: Your nightly Spark job runs for 2 hours on 1 TB. Data grows 100× over two years. What breaks first, and what is your plan?
points: Shuffle and skew grow faster than data: the widest join or aggregation breaks first
Full reprocessing stops fitting the window: move to incremental processing by partition
Small files and metadata growth slow the table; compaction and partition design matter
Cost grows with it: state the cost per run now and at 100×
Say what you would measure before changing anything

items.q: A Kafka topic carries 5,000 events a second today. Product wants 500,000. What breaks, in order?
points: Partition count caps consumer parallelism; adding partitions later reshuffles keys and order
Consumer lag and rebalances; state size in the stream processor
Broker disk and network; retention times throughput
Hot keys: one big city or merchant overloads one partition
Downstream sinks often break before Kafka does

items.q: A star schema serves 20 analysts well. The company grows to 2,000 users and 40 teams querying it. What breaks?
points: Concurrency and cost on the warehouse; workload isolation and caching
Conflicting metric definitions as teams add their own; a semantic layer or shared metrics
Wide fact tables and slowly changing dimensions grow; partition and cluster for the common filters
Ownership: who approves changes to shared dimensions

items.q: An LLM-based assistant answers 50 questions a day for one team. It is rolled out to 5,000 employees. What breaks?
points: Cost and rate limits; caching, smaller models for easy questions, budgets per team
Quality drift across many more question types; evals that grow with real questions
Access control: users must only retrieve what they are allowed to see
Latency and observability: tracing each answer to its sources

items.q: At 3 a.m. the nightly Python ingestion job is killed for using too much memory. It worked yesterday. Walk me through the first 15 minutes.
points: Stop the damage: is anything downstream reading partial data? Pause or mark the run failed clearly
Compare inputs: did today's file grow, change shape, or contain one giant record?
Check the last code or dependency change
Rerun safely only if the job is idempotent; otherwise fix the partial output first
Write down the follow-up: streaming the input and an alert on input size

items.q: The revenue dashboard shows yesterday's revenue doubled. The CFO has already seen it. Walk me through the first 15 minutes.
points: Assume a data problem until proven otherwise; tell stakeholders it is being checked, with a time for the next update
Check freshness and row counts by source and partition: duplicates from a rerun are the most common cause
Trace lineage from the dashboard back to the first table where the number is wrong
Fix forward or roll back the bad partition; then add the check that would have caught it (a uniqueness or volume test)

items.q: Consumer lag on the payments topic has grown for an hour and real-time fraud scores are 40 minutes late. What do you do?
points: Find whether input rose or processing slowed: compare produce rate and consume rate
Look for a poison message, a slow sink, a rebalance loop or one hot partition
Short term: scale consumers up to the partition count, skip to a dead-letter queue, or degrade to batch scoring
Communicate the business impact (fraud checks are late), then the fix and the follow-up

items.q: Your on-call agent posted a wrong root cause for a pipeline failure in the incident channel, and an engineer acted on it. What now?
points: Correct it in the channel first and stop the wrong action
Find why: missing evidence, a tool returning stale data, or the model guessing
Add an eval case from this incident; require the agent to cite evidence for each claim
Decide what the agent may do alone and what needs a human approval

items.q: For a 50 GB daily job, pick pandas, Polars, DuckDB or Spark, and say what you rejected and why.
points: Name the decision drivers: data size, team skills, where it runs, cost
A single-node engine (DuckDB or Polars) often wins at 50 GB on one machine: no cluster to run
Reject pandas for memory, and Spark for operational cost unless data or concurrency grows a lot
State the condition that would change your choice

items.q: The team wants Kafka for 200 events a minute from one service to one consumer. Approve or push back?
points: Push back unless replay, many consumers or ordering per key are needed soon
A queue (SQS) or a table with a poller is cheaper to run at this volume
Kafka's cost is operations: brokers, upgrades, schema registry, on-call
Say what future need would make Kafka the right call, and how to switch later

items.q: Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi for a new lakehouse used by Spark, Trino and Snowflake. Pick one and defend it.
points: Engine support decides first: which engines must read and write
Iceberg is the most engine-neutral; Delta is strongest inside Databricks; Hudi fits heavy upserts
Name what you give up with your pick
Mention catalog choice, because it matters as much as the table format

items.q: One big wide table or a star schema for the company's core business metrics? Defend your choice.
points: Star schema: one place to change a dimension, history kept, shared by many tables
Wide table: fast and simple for one use case, but duplicated logic and painful history
Often both: star as the source of truth, wide tables built from it for dashboards
Say who maintains each and what it costs to change

items.q: Databricks or Snowflake as the main platform for a 300-person company? You must pick one.
points: Start from the workloads: SQL analytics, data science, streaming, AI
Snowflake: less to operate, strong SQL and governance; Databricks: stronger for Spark, ML and open formats
Cost model and skills of the current team
State how you would keep the exit door open (open table formats)

items.q: Leadership asks whether the new in-app coaching feature is working. Define the metric, then the table that would compute it.
points: One north-star metric tied to the goal (for example, share of users who complete a practice session in week 2), plus guardrails
Define the grain: one row per user per day, or one row per session
Name the events needed and how late or duplicate events are handled
Say how you would avoid fooling yourself: a comparison group or a before-after with care

items.q: How would you know if shared rides (pooling) is working? Define the metrics, then model the fact table.
points: Metrics for riders (wait and trip time), drivers (earnings per hour) and the business (cost per trip), with one north star
Grain: one row per ride segment or per pooled trip, and why
Dimensions: rider, driver, zone, time; handle a trip whose riders change mid-route
Guardrails: cancellation rate and rider rating

items.q: Daily active users dropped 15% overnight. How do you find out whether it is real or a data problem?
points: Check data first: late or missing events by platform, app version and region
Compare with an independent source (logins, server logs)
If real, slice by segment to find where the drop sits
Report what you know, what you do not yet know, and when you will know

items.q: Forty pipelines across six teams produce three different revenue numbers. What is your plan for the next two quarters?
points: First month: inventory the pipelines and owners, and agree one definition of revenue with finance
Build one certified revenue table with tests and an owner; deprecate the others on a dated plan
Make the right way the easy way: a template and a metrics layer, not a policy document
Measure progress: number of certified metrics, number of retired pipelines, incidents

items.q: You join as the first data architect at a 500-person company with no data platform strategy. What do you do in your first 90 days?
points: Listen first: meet the main data consumers and producers, and list their top pains
Write a short current-state map and three to five principles
Pick one visible win in the first quarter
Deliver a strategy document with a roadmap, costs and what you will not do

items.q: Every team writes its pipelines in a different style and Python version, and on-call is painful. How do you fix that without slowing teams down?
points: A golden path: a template repo with the Python version, packaging, tests, logging and CI already set up
Make it the fastest way to start, not a mandate
Migrate the worst offenders first, measured by incidents
Keep an exception process for real needs

items.q: Cut the data platform bill by 40% this quarter without missing any service level. Where do you look first?
points: Measure first: cost by team, job and table (tagging and showback)
Biggest wins are usually idle clusters, oversized warehouses, full refreshes that could be incremental, and unused tables
Storage tiering and retention for old raw data
Agree with each team what service level it really needs

items.q: Your LLM features cost 30,000 dollars a month and finance wants it halved. What do you do?
points: Measure cost by feature and prompt
Cache repeated work, shorten prompts and context, route easy requests to smaller models
Batch offline work, cap tokens per request, set budgets per team
Check that quality does not drop with evals before and after

items.q: Warehouse costs doubled in six months while data grew 20%. What is going on, and what do you change?
points: Find the top queries and jobs by cost: often dashboards refreshing too often or full rebuilds
Clustering, materialised aggregates, and incremental models
Workload isolation and auto-suspend
Make cost visible to the teams who create it

items.q: Move the orders data from Postgres to a lakehouse with no downtime, and prove nothing was lost.
points: Initial snapshot plus change data capture from the same log position
Run both in parallel; reconcile counts and sums per day and per key
Switch readers one by one with a rollback plan
Decide when the old path is turned off, and who signs off

items.q: Migrate 300 Hive jobs to Spark on a lakehouse in the cloud over a year. How do you plan it?
points: Inventory and group the jobs by pattern; automate the common patterns
Migrate by business domain with a parallel run and automated comparison
Freeze new development on the old platform with a date
Track progress and cost every month; keep the team who owns each job involved

items.q: A critical pipeline is a 4,000-line Python script nobody wants to touch. How do you replace it safely?
points: Characterisation tests: capture its outputs on real inputs first
Strangle it: move one part at a time behind the same interface
Run old and new side by side and compare outputs
Remove the old part only when the comparison has been clean for a while

items.q: 2 million ride events a minute, 1 KB each. How many Kafka partitions, and how much storage a day with 7 days of retention and replication 3?
points: About 33,000 events a second, about 33 MB a second
At around 5 to 10 MB a second per partition consumer, roughly 8 to 16 partitions, more for headroom and peaks
About 2.9 TB a day raw; times 3 replicas and 7 days is about 60 TB
State the assumptions out loud and round

items.q: How much memory does a Python dict with 50 million string keys and integer values need? Would you hold it in memory?
points: Each entry costs the key string object, the int object and the hash table slot: roughly 100 bytes or more per entry
So about 5 GB or more: too big for many workers
Alternatives: a sorted array, a database, DuckDB, or processing by partition
Say how you would measure it (tracemalloc) instead of guessing

items.q: A fact table gets 500 million rows a day at 200 bytes a row in Parquet. How big is a year, and how would you partition it?
points: About 100 GB a day uncompressed, maybe 20 to 30 GB compressed; around 10 TB a year compressed
Partition by day (or hour if queries are hourly); avoid partitions smaller than about 1 GB
Cluster by the common filter columns
Plan retention and compaction

items.q: Walk me through the most complex data system you built: why each main choice, what failed, and what you would change now.
points: A one-minute overview: the business problem, scale and your role
Two or three key decisions with the alternatives you rejected
One real failure and what you changed afterwards
What you would do differently today, and the measurable impact

items.q: Tell me about a design decision you got wrong. How did you find out, and what did you do?
points: Pick a real decision with consequences
How you detected it (metrics, incidents, user feedback)
How you fixed it and communicated it
What you do differently now

items.q: Another team's design will hurt your platform, and you do not manage them. What do you do?
points: Understand their goals and constraints first
Bring data: the cost or risk to your platform, in their terms
Offer an alternative that meets their goal, and agree a decision maker
Disagree and commit if the decision goes against you, with the risk written down

items.q: A senior engineer on your team keeps shipping pipelines without tests and says they slow him down. How do you handle it?
points: Talk one to one about outcomes: incidents and rework, not rules
Make testing cheap: templates and examples
Agree a clear standard for the team, applied to everyone
Follow up and recognise the change

items.q: You must say no to a VP who wants a real-time dashboard by next week. How do you handle it?
points: Ask what decision the dashboard supports and how fresh the data truly needs to be
Offer options with dates: hourly next week, real time in a quarter
Be clear about the cost and risk of rushing
Confirm the agreement in writing

items.q: Design a payments-style write API that is safe to retry. What exactly makes it idempotent?
points: The client sends an idempotency key with each request
The server stores the key and the result in the same transaction as the write; a repeated key returns the stored result
Keys expire after a window; a unique constraint backs it up
Say what happens if two requests with the same key arrive at the same moment (a lock or insert-first on the key)

items.q: Backfill a new column on a two-billion-row table that takes writes all day, without hurting production.
points: Expand, write to both (CDC or a trigger), backfill, verify, switch reads, contract
Small primary-key batches, each committed, resumable from the last id, idempotent
Throttle on replication lag and load; never one giant transaction or OFFSET paging
Rollback stays possible until the old structure is dropped

items.q: A metrics API in front of the warehouse serves 50 requests a second. A new app launch will bring 5,000. What do you put in front of it?
points: A cache with invalidation on data refresh and a time-to-live; protect against a thundering herd
Precomputed aggregates for the common queries
Rate limits per client and a circuit breaker in front of the warehouse
Horizontal API servers behind a load balancer; say what the warehouse itself can take

items.q: Design surge pricing for one city: estimate the event rate and state size, then say how you would flag drivers behaving oddly.
points: Estimate drivers and riders online, location pings per second and zones; state per zone is small
A streaming job aggregates supply and demand per zone per minute; price comes from the ratio, smoothed
Anomalies: compare each driver with recent fare-per-km and acceptance baselines; beware drivers who just lost network
Say what runs in real time and what runs in batch, and how you would test it

items.q: A clickstream pipeline handles 50,000 events a second today. Marketing plans a launch that brings 2 million a second for a week. What breaks first, in order, and what do you change?
points: Partition count: at a few MB/s per partition, 2 GB/s needs hundreds of partitions; repartitioning a live topic reshuffles keys, so create a new topic sized for peak and cut producers over
Consumers: one task per partition, so stream jobs need matching parallelism and state backends sized for the larger key space
Sinks: the lake gets millions of small files and the serving store gets write hot spots; batch writes, compact hourly, salt hot keys
Broker disks and network with replication factor 3, and retention: shorten it or turn on tiered storage
Say what you test first: a load test at 2× the forecast, and which dashboards you accept being minutes stale during the launch

items.q: Your Iceberg lake has 3 PB and query planning now takes longer than the queries. Why, and what do you change?
points: Planning reads manifests: millions of small files and long snapshot histories make the metadata tree huge
Compact data files to 512 MB to 1 GB and rewrite manifests so each covers a partition range
Expire old snapshots and remove orphan files on a schedule, keeping enough history for time travel and audits
Partition for the filters people use (hidden partitioning by day, sort by the next filter column) so pruning skips most manifests
Measure before and after: planning time, files scanned per query, and the catalog's request rate

items.q: Your VP wants to replace the warehouse with a lakehouse to save money. Defend a position.
points: Start from workloads: concurrent BI, ad hoc, ML training, streaming; the answer differs per workload
Open tables (Iceberg, Delta) cut storage cost and lock-in and let several engines share one copy; the warehouse still wins on high-concurrency dashboards and zero tuning
Hidden costs: running engines, compaction, governance and people; compare total cost, not storage price
A likely answer: lake as the system of record, a warehouse or OLAP store for hot marts, one catalog and access policy for both
Say how you would prove it: migrate one domain, measure cost per query and freshness, then decide

items.q: A team proposes dual writes (to the database and to Kafka in the same request) instead of CDC. Approve or push back.
points: Dual writes fail halfway: the database commits and Kafka fails, or the reverse, and the two disagree silently
Log-based CDC (Debezium) reads committed changes, so Kafka matches the database without touching app code
If they need business events rather than row changes, use the outbox pattern: write the event in the same transaction, CDC ships it
CDC costs: connector operations, WAL retention when the connector lags, schema changes
Decision: push back on dual writes; outbox plus CDC gives the same events safely

items.q: At 2 a.m. the Postgres primary's disk is 95% full and climbing. Nothing changed in the app. What do you check first?
points: Replication slots: a stalled CDC connector or dead replica holds WAL forever; pg_replication_slots shows lag in bytes
Act: restart or fix the connector; if it cannot catch up before the disk fills, drop the slot and plan a re-snapshot (say the cost)
Other causes: long-running transactions blocking vacuum, a runaway temp table, logs
Prevent it: alert on slot lag in bytes, cap WAL retention for slots (max_slot_wal_keep_size), and page the connector's owner
Afterwards: a blameless review and a runbook entry

items.q: A Flink job's checkpoint times are rising and the job restarts every hour. Consumer lag is growing. Walk me through it.
points: Look at backpressure and the slowest operator first; checkpoints wait for barriers behind backpressure
Check state size growth: a window or join without TTL keeps every key forever
Check skew: one subtask with far more records (a hot key) slows every checkpoint
Fixes: state TTL, incremental checkpoints with RocksDB, unaligned checkpoints under backpressure, salting the hot key, more parallelism up to the partition count
Protect the business meanwhile: tell consumers the data is late, and alert on checkpoint duration before it fails

items.q: The CFO's revenue dashboard shows yesterday at half its usual value. It is 7 a.m. What do you do?
points: First, is the data late or wrong? Check freshness and row counts per source against a normal day
Common causes: a partition that did not land, a join that dropped rows after a dimension change, a currency or timezone change
Communicate early: a banner on the dashboard and a message to the CFO's team with an estimate
Fix forward: rerun the affected partition idempotently, then reconcile totals with the finance source
Prevent: volume and freshness checks that block publishing, and a certified metric with an owner

items.q: An S3-backed job starts failing with 503 Slow Down errors after a new partitioning scheme went live. Diagnose and fix.
points: S3 limits request rate per prefix (about 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads a second); the new scheme probably puts all writes under one prefix
Confirm with the request metrics per prefix or the error spread over keys
Fix: spread keys over prefixes (hash or high-cardinality first component), and write fewer, larger files
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter keep the job alive meanwhile
Add a load test of the write path when partitioning changes

items.q: Uber Eats: how would you measure whether a new restaurant ranking helps the marketplace, not just clicks?
points: Goal: more completed orders that customers rate well, without starving smaller restaurants or slowing deliveries
Primary: completed orders per session; guardrails: delivery time, cancellation rate, share of orders to new restaurants
Experiment unit: users, but watch interference (courier supply is shared), so consider city-level switchback tests
Data: impression log with rank position, orders joined by session, a daily fact per user and variant
Decide in advance the minimum effect worth shipping and the run time

items.q: Meta: Reels watch time is up 8% but daily active users are flat. Is the product doing well?
points: Check definitions: watch time per user or total; did a logging change inflate it (autoplay counted)?
Segment: is the gain concentrated in heavy users while light users churn?
Look for cannibalisation: did feed or messaging time fall by the same amount?
Long-term signals: retention at 7 and 28 days, creator posting, satisfaction surveys
Conclude with what you would recommend measuring next and which guardrail would make you stop

items.q: Salesforce: define the metrics and the data model for customer health across thousands of tenant orgs.
points: Health = adoption (weekly active users / licences), depth (key features used), outcomes (cases closed, deals won), and risk (support tickets, contract end)
Grain: one row per org per week, a periodic snapshot, with a score and its parts
Sources: product events per tenant, licence and billing data, support cases; tenant id on everything
Dimensions: org (Type 2 on segment and owner), product, date
Validate the score: does it predict renewals? Back-test before anyone uses it

items.q: Google Maps: offline maps downloads are up 30% after a release. Prove it is real before you celebrate.
points: Check logging first: a new event name, double firing, retries counted as downloads
Compare with server-side bytes served and storage used on devices
Segment by app version, platform and country to find where the change is
Check the release itself: did a prompt push downloads users never use? Measure offline sessions after download
Report the real effect with a confidence interval and what changed in usage

items.q: Define and pipeline a real-time driver supply metric for a ride-hailing city operations team.
points: Metric: available drivers per geo cell per minute versus open requests (supply-demand ratio), plus ETA to pickup
Events: driver_status (online, available, on trip) with location every few seconds; ride requests
Pipeline: Kafka keyed by driver; a stream job keeps each driver's latest state and counts per cell per minute
Serve to a real-time OLAP store for dashboards; land raw events for daily history
Edge cases: GPS noise, drivers toggling status, late events, cells with few drivers

items.q: Three product teams each built their own customer table with different numbers. How do you fix it without stopping them?
points: Find the definitions and the consumers; agree on one owner for customer data
Publish one certified customer table with a contract, tests and documented semantics
Migrate consumers team by team with a diff report; keep the old tables read-only for a period
Make it the easy path: a golden path template, catalog listing, and access by default
Measure: number of copies over time and incidents from mismatched numbers

items.q: The data platform team is a ticket queue: every request waits two weeks. How do you change that?
points: Find the top request types; most are repetitive (new source, new table, access)
Turn them into self-service with guardrails: templates, a CLI or UI, automatic checks
Define what the platform owns versus domain teams (data mesh style responsibilities)
Set service levels and publish them; reserve capacity for platform work
Measure lead time per request type before and after

items.q: Incidents keep coming from the same pipelines but nobody owns them. What do you put in place?
points: An owner for every pipeline and table in the catalog, with an on-call rotation
Service levels for the important datasets (freshness, completeness) with alerts that page the owner
Blameless post-incident reviews with tracked actions
Retire or hand over orphans: no owner, no production status
Report incident counts and time to recover per domain monthly

items.q: You join as the first staff data engineer in a 40-person data org. What do you do in your first 90 days?
points: Listen: meet consumers and teams, read incident history, map the systems and costs
Find the two or three problems with the most pain and leverage, with numbers
Write a short strategy document: where we are, where we go, what we will not do
Ship one visible win early to earn trust, while starting the longer change
Build the habits: design reviews, ownership, standards

items.q: Analysts and engineers disagree about who owns transformation logic. Settle it.
points: Split by layer: engineers own ingestion and core models with contracts; analysts own marts on top
One tool and repository for transformations (dbt), with code review for both groups
Tests and contracts at the boundary so changes below do not break marts silently
Shared on-call for certified marts; experimental work stays in sandboxes
Write it down and revisit in a quarter

items.q: Your BigQuery bill doubled in a month. Find the cause and cut it.
points: Look at the job history: top queries and users by bytes scanned; usually a few dashboards or a scheduled query
Fix scans: partition by date, cluster by filter columns, require partition filters on big tables
Pre-aggregate the dashboard queries into a small daily table
Consider capacity pricing (slots) if spend is steady; set quotas per project
Report savings in dollars a month and set an alert on spend

items.q: Storage is now the largest line on your cloud bill: 8 PB of S3. How do you cut it by half?
points: Know what is there: an inventory by prefix, age and last access
Lifecycle rules: infrequent access after 30 days, archive after 180 for raw data you rarely read
Delete what nobody needs: old snapshots, temp data, duplicate copies; set retention by dataset
Compress and compact: Parquet with zstd, fewer small files (also cuts request costs)
Check retrieval costs and legal holds before archiving

items.q: Spark jobs run on on-demand clusters 24 hours a day. How do you lower the cost without missing SLAs?
points: Measure utilisation: most clusters idle much of the day
Autoscaling and job clusters that shut down after the run
Spot capacity for restartable batch work with a fallback to on-demand
Right-size executors (memory and cores) from the Spark UI; fix skew and spills that waste time
Track cost per job and per table so owners see it

items.q: Your streaming platform runs 300 Flink jobs. Finance asks why it costs more than the batch platform. Answer them.
points: Streaming pays for always-on compute; batch pays only while running
List jobs by cost and freshness need; many do not need seconds
Move minutes-fresh use cases to micro-batch or scheduled incremental jobs
Consolidate small jobs, scale down at night, right-size state backends
Show the trade-off in a table: freshness, cost, risk

items.q: Cross-region data transfer is 20% of the bill. What do you do?
points: Find the flows: replication, consumers in another region, backups
Keep compute next to the data; read replicas or copies only where needed
Compress and filter before transfer; replicate aggregates instead of raw data
Check if multi-region is required at all for each dataset (RPO and RTO needs)
Price it: about $20 per TB between regions, so name the savings

items.q: Move 500 tables from an on-premises Oracle warehouse to the cloud with no downtime for reporting.
points: Inventory tables, jobs and consumers; group by domain
Initial bulk copy plus CDC to keep the cloud copy current
Rebuild jobs in the new platform domain by domain, run both and diff results automatically
Cut over consumers per domain with a rollback path; keep the old system read-only until signed off
Track progress and cost in a dashboard everyone sees

items.q: Upgrade a Kafka cluster used by 200 services from ZooKeeper mode to KRaft without an outage.
points: Read the supported path: upgrade to a bridge version, migrate metadata to KRaft controllers, then remove ZooKeeper
Test in a staging cluster with production-like traffic and clients
Roll brokers one at a time with health checks (under-replicated partitions zero before the next)
Communicate with service owners; freeze topic changes during the window
Rollback plan for each phase and what you monitor

items.q: Replace hand-written SQL scripts scheduled by cron with dbt and an orchestrator.
points: Inventory the scripts and their outputs; find dependencies from table reads
Port by domain into dbt models with tests; keep output tables identical
Run both and compare row counts and sums daily until they match
Move scheduling to the orchestrator with retries and alerts
Delete cron jobs only after a quiet period

items.q: Change the partitioning of a 1 PB table that hundreds of jobs read, without breaking them.
points: With Iceberg, partition evolution changes the spec for new data without rewriting old data
Readers using hidden partitioning keep working; jobs that read file paths directly need changes, so find them
Rewrite old partitions in the background if queries need the new layout
Watch query performance and file counts during the change
Announce it with a date and a contact

items.q: Estimate the storage and compute for keeping 13 months of 50 billion ad impressions a day.
points: 50 billion × 200 bytes = 10 TB a day raw; Parquet about 2 TB a day; 13 months about 800 TB
Storage at about $23 a TB-month is about $18,000 a month standard; colder tiers for older months
Daily aggregation reads 2 TB; at about 50 MB/s per vCPU that is about 11 vCPU-hours, cheap
Queries over all history are the cost: pre-aggregate by campaign and day
State the assumptions and check the biggest one

items.q: How many Debezium connectors and Kafka partitions for 200 databases doing 50,000 changes a second in total?
points: One connector per database (they read one log each); 200 connectors over a Connect cluster
50,000 changes × 1 KB = 50 MB/s; partitions per table by key, a few partitions per busy table
Busiest database decides connector throughput; a single connector does a few thousand changes a second
WAL retention for the slowest connector's downtime
Monitor lag per connector

items.q: Estimate the cost to embed 1 billion documents and serve similarity search for them.
points: Tokens: 1 billion × 500 tokens = 500 billion tokens; at a hosted price per million tokens, multiply out (say the price you assume)
Vectors: 1 billion × 768 dimensions × 4 bytes ≈ 3 TB; with compression (quantisation) much less
Index memory for approximate search; shard across nodes
Re-embedding on model change is the hidden cost: plan for it
Compare self-hosted GPU embedding at volume

items.q: How big is the warehouse for 5,000 analysts running 200 queries each a day?
points: 1 million queries a day; peak maybe 100 at once in office hours
Most are small; a few heavy ones dominate cost; separate workloads (warehouses or slot reservations)
Estimate bytes scanned per query from partitioning; turn into cost per month
Cache and pre-aggregate dashboards
Say how you would measure in the first week and resize

items.q: Walk me through the most complex pipeline you own, from source to consumer, with its numbers.
points: Sources, volume (events a second, bytes a day), freshness target and consumers
The flow box by box, and why each box is there
Its failure modes and how you detect them
What it costs a month and what drives the cost
What you would change if you rebuilt it

items.q: Tell me about a time you chose between building and buying a data tool. What did you decide and why?
points: The need and the options compared, with numbers (cost, time, risk)
Who would own it and run it
What you decided and the trade-off you accepted
How it turned out, with evidence
What you would do differently

items.q: Describe a data correctness bug that reached a business decision. How did it happen and what changed?
points: The bug and how it was found
Why tests and checks missed it
Impact in business terms and how you communicated
The fix and the checks you added
What you changed in process

items.q: Pick a system you designed. What happens at ten times the load?
points: Current numbers and the first bottleneck
The second and third bottlenecks
What you would change and at what scale
What it would cost
How you would test it

items.q: Tell me about the largest cost saving you delivered. How did you find it?
points: Where the money went and how you measured it
The changes, ranked by saving and risk
How you kept service levels
The result in dollars a month
How you kept it from creeping back

items.q: Describe your worst production incident. What did you learn?
points: What happened and the impact
How it was detected and the timeline
The root cause and contributing factors
What you changed to prevent it
What you learned about yourself or the team

items.q: Two senior engineers disagree strongly about a design and the team is stuck. What do you do?
points: Write the options down with criteria agreed first (cost, risk, time, operability)
Let each present; find what evidence would change minds and get it quickly (a spike or load test)
Decide, or name who decides, with a date
Record the decision and the reasons (an ADR)
Check later whether it worked; no blame

items.q: How do you grow senior engineers into staff engineers on your team?
points: Give them problems bigger than one team, with real ownership
Coach on writing (design docs, strategy) and influence
Sponsor them in rooms they are not in yet
Feedback with examples, regularly
Celebrate their wins publicly

items.q: A product director wants a feature in two weeks that you think needs two months to do safely. How do you handle it?
points: Understand the goal behind the date
Offer options: a smaller version in two weeks, the full one later, and the risks of each
Make the risk concrete with numbers
Agree on the plan in writing
Deliver what you promised and report

items.q: How do you set technical direction for data across several teams you do not manage?
points: A short written strategy with principles and a few bets
Bring others in early so it is theirs too
Make the right thing easy (templates, platforms)
Review designs and give useful feedback
Measure adoption and adjust

items.q: Tell me about a time you changed your mind after a junior engineer pushed back.
points: The situation and your initial view
What they said and how you listened
What evidence changed your mind
The outcome
What it taught you about leading
